title: IMF Warns an AI Share Crash Could Test the Limits of Global Resilience
excerpt: The Fund's stability report flags $650 billion of AI-linked debt, circular financing between tech giants and surging hyperscaler bond issuance as vulnerabilities that could turn an earnings miss into a global selloff.
body:
• The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report names an AI share-price correction as one of three "salient risks" to world financial stability, alongside rising government borrowing costs and a major cyber-attack.
  • The Fund counted $300 billion in equity deals and $650 billion in debt across 14 transactions between hyperscalers and weaker AI firms over three years, against $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments.
  • Hyperscalers now account for 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024 — leverage that could turn an AI earnings miss into forced selling across markets.
  • For diaspora investors concentrated in US tech stocks, the IMF's warning is specific: an AI correction's consequences "could be global," with the US and Asian markets most exposed.

The International Monetary Fund has warned that a crash in artificial intelligence share prices could ripple across world markets, naming an AI correction one of three plausible near-term catalysts for "a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil" in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report. The other two: a spike in government borrowing costs and a large-scale cyber-attack.

"The consequences of an AI correction could be global."

— International Monetary Fund, Global Financial Stability Report

The leverage underneath the boom

The Fund's concern is less the technology than the financing wrapped around it. It highlighted the interconnectedness of the big AI companies and the debt funding their investment: 14 deals among the largest firms over three years totalled $300 billion in equity investment and $650 billion in debt, in exchange for $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments. Hyperscalers — the largest data-centre operators — now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024, according to the report as covered by Reuters. "Circular financing arrangements" — equity and debt flowing between AI firms that are also each other's customers — mean stress at one company can lower revenue forecasts and valuations across the chain.

The IMF also pointed to "growing evidence" that AI's successful rollout may not require investment on the scale now under way, and that the economic gains may be smaller than expected. If AI profits or investment wane, rising leverage, concentrated exposures and retail investors borrowing to speculate could amplify a correction into broader volatility.

A resilient economy, under strain

The stability warning arrived with the Fund's World Economic Outlook, which projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027. "The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks to growth tilted to the downside," said chief economist Silvana Tenreyro. The report describes a bifurcated outlook: AI investment has propped up growth, but the war in the Middle East has pushed refined petroleum prices 70-95% above pre-war levels, hitting energy-importing countries hardest. India, which the Fund upgraded to 7% growth, is the standout exception — as our companion report details.

What it means for investors

The IMF called on policymakers to curb excessive leverage, including derivatives and margin loans. For individual investors — and Indian diaspora portfolios are heavily weighted toward US mega-cap tech — the practical reading is about concentration, not prediction: the Fund is not forecasting a crash, but it is saying the system's shock absorbers are thinner than the headline indices suggest, because so much growth, borrowing and market value now rest on one technology theme.

What's next

The near-term tests are earnings: hyperscaler results this season will be read against the debt they have issued, and any guidance cut lands on a market the IMF says is primed to amplify it. Sovereign yields are the second tripwire — a loss of fiscal credibility in a major economy, the Fund warns, would make global growth materially lower than its baseline.
